analysis.one_liner: Lets anyone put 401(k)-sized amounts in tax-free health accounts and spend them on insurance, vitamins, and gym fees.
analysis.headline: A single senator introduced the bill in December 2025; it has zero cosponsors and has sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise health savings account (HSA) contribution limits to the same level as 401(k) retirement plans, drop the rule that a person must be enrolled in a high-deductible health plan to have an HSA, and let account money pay for health insurance premiums, direct primary care, vitamins, dietary supplements, gym memberships, and fitness trackers — all tax-free. It would also let new 'health marketplace pools' — groups of individuals and small employers banded together — count as an 'employer' under federal benefits law, so they can buy group-style health plans, including plans that cover nothing but prescription drugs. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and has had no action since [S2][S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income households with thousands of dollars of spare cash to shelter in an HSA gain the largest tax deductions — the contribution limit rises to roughly 401(k) levels (over $23,000 per year, plus a catch-up for those 50 and older). Healthy self-employed people and small employers gain access to group-style plans through the new marketplace pools. Health insurers gain new enrollment channels, and makers of vitamins, supplements, gym memberships, and fitness trackers gain a tax-free customer base [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, insurers, supplement and fitness sellers

how_it_helps.text: Raises annual HSA contribution limits to the same dollar amount as 401(k) plans, with an additional catch-up contribution for people 50 and older — a far larger limit than today's HSA caps [S2].

Removes the requirement that a person be enrolled in a high-deductible health plan to contribute to an HSA, so anyone with taxable income can fund one, and lets account money pay for health insurance premiums and direct primary care arrangements [S2].
Makes vitamins, dietary supplements, gym memberships, and wearable fitness trackers 'qualified medical expenses' that can be paid from an HSA tax-free [S2].

Lets 'health marketplace pools' of individuals and small employers be treated as an employer under ERISA, so they can offer group health plans — including plans that cover prescription or over-the-counter drugs as the only benefit [S2].
Adds bankruptcy protections for HSAs equal to retirement accounts and lets account holders roll over balances to children, parents, or grandparents [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through lost revenue: every dollar deducted into an HSA and spent tax-free — including on gym memberships and supplements — is revenue the Treasury does not collect. If healthier people move into narrow pool plans or drug-only coverage, the cost of covering the sick in broader insurance pools can rise. People with chronic conditions benefit least from a savings-based system because they spend rather than save [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal Treasury and sicker insurance enrollees

drawbacks.text: Tax deductions are worth most to people in high tax brackets who can set aside tens of thousands of dollars a year; a family living paycheck to paycheck gets little or nothing from the same deduction [S2].

The bill removes any link between the accounts and actual health coverage — a person can contribute tax-free without holding any insurance — and the new marketplace pools may offer plans covering nothing but drugs, which could pull healthier people out of broad insurance risk pools and raise premiums for those who remain [S2].

Letting gym memberships, vitamins, and dietary supplements count as tax-free medical spending converts general consumer purchases into a federal tax subsidy with no requirement of medical necessity [S2].

The marketplace-pool language keeps insurers' ability to underwrite and exclude or limit coverage for individuals, subject to existing federal portability rules, meaning these new group-style plans would not necessarily cover everyone at the same price [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is real help here for self-employed people and small employers who want cheaper, pooled coverage, and for savers who want flexibility. But the tax benefit scales with income: a top-bracket household sheltering the full new limit saves several thousand dollars a year, while a household that cannot spare the cash saves nothing. The cost — forgone federal revenue and thinner, pricier risk pools for the sick — falls on everyone else. On balance the bill's largest and most certain beneficiaries are higher-income households and the industries whose products become tax-advantaged.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.

narrative.text: Rand Paul (R-KY) introduced S. 3362 in the Senate on December 4, 2025 [S1].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S4].
No senator has cosponsored the bill [S3].
The Finance Committee has taken no further action on the bill, and no vote has occurred [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has changed yet: because the bill has not advanced, the current tax treatment of health spending and the current insurance market rules remain in place, and no one has gained. If it ever moved, the biggest winners would be high-income households able to shelter the new larger amounts, followed by insurers and the supplement and fitness industries.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet — the bill has not advanced

for.name: Rand Paul
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kentucky; introduced the bill
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced S. 3362 in the Senate, sending it to the Finance Committee

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; the bill's only recorded support is its single Republican sponsor, with zero cosponsors from either party [S3].

industries.note: The bill opens new sales channels: HSA money may pay premiums, and 'health marketplace pools' can buy group coverage through insurers, including drug-only plans. Insurers gain customers whether the plans are broad or narrow, though narrow plans can raise costs for everyone else's coverage.

Contribution limits rise to 401(k) levels with no coverage requirement, so a top-bracket household can shelter over $23,000 a year tax-free. The forgone revenue is borne by all federal taxpayers, and households unable to spare cash get nothing.

Their products become tax-free 'qualified medical expenses,' effectively a federal subsidy on their sales. Buyers gain the same deduction, but the Treasury loses revenue on spending with no medical-necessity requirement.

industries.industry: Gyms and wearable fitness tracker makers
industries.note: Membership and device purchases become tax-deductible medical spending. Ordinary buyers share the benefit, but general consumer goods are being reclassified as health care at public cost.

Patients may pay fixed periodic fees for primary care from an HSA pre-tax, putting more money into subscription-style primary care practices. Patients who use these arrangements gain tax-free treatment of routine care.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee action since referral, the bill is very likely to sit without a hearing until this Congress ends in January 2027, as do most bills referred to committee with no co-sponsorship.
